english: being deeply moved; overwhelming emotion (often to tears)
usage: a surge of feeling far stronger than ordinary being-touched
verb form; 감격했어요 = I was overwhelmed with emotion
adjective; 감격스러운 순간 = an overwhelming moment
set phrase, often at reunions or victories
examples: 10년 만에 가족을 다시 만나서 감격했어요.
I was overwhelmed with emotion at reuniting with my family after ten years.
감격하다 = to be deeply moved
우승이 확정되는 순간 선수들은 감격의 눈물을 흘렸어요.
The moment the championship was sealed, the players shed tears of deep emotion.
감격의 눈물 = tears of deep emotion
힘든 시간을 견디고 합격해서 정말 감격스러웠어요.
After enduring a hard time I passed, so it was truly overwhelming.
감격스럽다 = to be deeply moving
nuance: 감격 is being overwhelmed with emotion, a far more intense surge than the everyday 감동 (being touched). It is the welling-up you feel at a long-awaited reunion, a hard-won victory, or a dream finally realized, often bringing tears. The verb 감격하다 and phrase 감격의 눈물 are core; reserve 감격 for genuinely powerful, climactic moments rather than mildly touching ones.
mistakes: Using 감격 for any touching moment; it is reserved for an overwhelming surge, while ordinary 'I was moved' is closer to 뭉클했어요
Saying just 감격이에요 to describe a thing; for the adjective use 감격스럽다 (감격스러운 순간)

usage: the noun; the verb is 만족하다
examples: 새로 산 노트북 성능에 아주 만족해요.
I'm very satisfied with the performance of the laptop I just bought.
N에 만족하다 = satisfied with N
이번 여행은 날씨도 좋고 음식도 맛있어서 만족스러웠어요.
This trip was satisfying because the weather was nice and the food was good.
만족스럽다 = to be satisfying
작은 일에도 만족할 줄 아는 사람이 행복한 것 같아요.
I think people who know how to be content even with small things are happy.
만족할 줄 알다 = to know how to be satisfied
nuance: 만족 is contentment, the settled feeling that something is good enough or has met your expectations. The key pattern is N에 만족하다 ('to be satisfied with N'), so watch the particle 에. Use 만족스럽다 to describe the thing itself as satisfying (만족스러운 결과), while 만족하다 describes the person's state.
mistakes: Using the particle 을/를 instead of 에; it is N에 만족하다, not N을 만족하다
Confusing 만족 (satisfaction) with 만끽 (savoring/enjoying to the full); they are different words

examples: 회사 복지에 대해 불만이 좀 있어요.
I have some complaints about the company's benefits.
N에 대해 불만이 있다 = to have complaints about N
그렇게 불만만 말하지 말고 개선 방법을 찾아봐요.
Instead of just voicing complaints, let's look for ways to improve.
불만만 말하다 = to only complain
사소한 일에도 불만이 많은 사람과는 일하기 힘들어요.
It's hard to work with someone who has many complaints even over trivial things.
불만이 많다 = to have many complaints
nuance: 불만 is dissatisfaction, the grievance you feel when something falls short, and the direct antonym of 만족. It pairs with 있다/많다 and the phrase N에 대해 불만이 있다 ('to have a complaint about N'). 불만 is the inner feeling or expressed gripe, distinct from 불평, which leans toward the act of grumbling out loud.
mistakes: Saying 불만하다; the noun pairs with 있다/많다/가지다, not 하다
Confusing it with 불안 (anxiety); 불만 is dissatisfaction, 불안 is uneasy worry

usage: feeling for someone in a hard situation
the trait; 동정심이 많다 = very compassionate
examples: 저는 동정이 아니라 진심으로 도와드리고 싶은 거예요.
It's not pity, I genuinely want to help you.
동정이 아니라 = not out of pity
뉴스를 보면서 그 가족에게 동정심을 느꼈어요.
Watching the news, I felt compassion for that family.
동정심을 느끼다 = to feel compassion
동정 받는 게 싫어서 힘든 티를 안 냈어요.
I hated being pitied, so I didn't show that I was struggling.
동정 받다 = to be pitied
nuance: 동정 is sympathy or pity for someone in a difficult situation, often tinged with a sense of looking down, which is why people say 동정 아니야 ('it's not pity') to soften it. The trait noun 동정심 (compassion) is warmer and more positive. Be careful: telling someone you 동정해요 can sound condescending, so 안타깝다 or 마음이 아프다 is often gentler.
mistakes: Using 동정 freely for warm sympathy; it can imply pitying from above, so be careful with tone
Confusing it with 공감 (empathy); 동정 feels for someone, 공감 feels with them

english: compassion; deep pity; empathy for suffering
examples: 주인공의 사연을 알고 나니 연민이 느껴졌어요.
Once I learned the protagonist's backstory, I felt compassion.
연민이 느껴지다 = compassion is felt
그는 길고양이에게 깊은 연민을 느끼는 사람이에요.
He's someone who feels deep compassion for stray cats.
깊은 연민 = deep compassion
미워하던 마음이 어느새 연민으로 바뀌었어요.
The resentment I'd felt turned into compassion before I knew it.
연민으로 바뀌다 = to turn into compassion
nuance: 연민 is a deeper, more literary compassion, the ache you feel witnessing another's suffering. It is warmer and weightier than 동정 and carries less of the condescending edge, appearing often in novels, film reviews, and reflective writing. 연민을 느끼다 is the core phrase; intermediate learners meet this word mostly in written or thoughtful spoken Korean.
mistakes: Using it in casual chat where 안쓰럽다 or 안타깝다 fits better; 연민 sounds literary
Saying 연민하다; pair the noun with 느끼다/들다, not 하다

usage: looking up to someone's character or achievement
존경하는 선생님 = a teacher I respect
passive; 존경받는 사람 = a respected person
examples: 저는 끝까지 포기하지 않는 그분을 정말 존경해요.
I truly respect that person who never gives up.
존경하다 = to respect
힘든 일을 묵묵히 해내는 부모님께 존경심을 느껴요.
I feel respect for my parents, who quietly get hard things done.
존경심을 느끼다 = to feel respect
그 교수님은 학생들에게 존경받는 분이에요.
That professor is someone respected by the students.
존경받다 = to be respected
nuance: 존경 is deep respect or admiration directed at a person, for their character, effort, or achievements, and is stronger than mere 인정 (acknowledgment). You'll often hear 존경하는 ('respected') before a title in speeches and letters, and 존경받는 사람 is high praise. It refers to people, not things; for valuing an abstract thing you'd use 중요하게 여기다 instead.
mistakes: Using 존경 for objects or ideas; it targets people you look up to
Confusing it with 존중 (respecting others' rights/opinions); 존경 is admiration, 존중 is treating with respect

usage: positive pride in what you do or belong to
describes someone proud of their work
examples: 저는 제 일에 자부심을 가지고 있어요.
I take pride in my work.
N에 자부심을 가지다 = to take pride in N
우리 팀은 결과물에 대한 자부심이 강해요.
Our team has strong pride in what we produce.
자부심이 강하다 = to have strong pride
오랜 노력 끝에 자격증을 따서 자부심을 느꼈어요.
After long effort I earned the certificate, so I felt proud.
자부심을 느끼다 = to feel pride
nuance: 자부심 is healthy, positive pride in your own work, skill, or group, the good kind of pride, unlike the easily wounded ego of 자존심. The natural pattern is N에 자부심을 가지다 ('to take pride in N'). Saying you have 자부심 about your job or team is admirable in Korean, signaling dedication rather than arrogance.
mistakes: Confusing 자부심 (positive pride in achievement) with 자존심 (defensive ego)
Saying 자부심하다; pair the noun with 가지다/느끼다, not 하다

usage: the noun; the verb is 절망하다
examples: 시험에 또 떨어져서 잠깐 절망에 빠졌어요.
I failed the exam again, so I briefly fell into despair.
절망에 빠지다 = to fall into despair
상황이 절망적이어도 포기하지 않으려고 해요.
Even if the situation is hopeless, I try not to give up.
절망적이다 = to be hopeless
그 소식을 듣고 절망하기엔 아직 일러요.
It's still too early to despair over that news.
절망하다 = to despair
nuance: 절망 is despair, the heavy collapse of hope, and the strong opposite of 희망. It pairs vividly with 빠지다 (절망에 빠지다, 'to fall into despair') and yields the adjective 절망적이다 for hopeless situations. This is a heavy, dramatic word; for everyday letdowns 실망 (disappointment) is far more appropriate.
mistakes: Confusing 절망 (despair, total loss of hope) with 실망 (disappointment, a letdown)
Overusing it for minor setbacks; 절망 is reserved for genuinely hopeless feelings

usage: the soothing of a troubled heart
examples: 힘들 때 친구의 말 한마디가 큰 위안이 됐어요.
When I was struggling, a single word from my friend was a great comfort.
위안이 되다 = to be a comfort
혼자가 아니라는 사실에서 위안을 얻었어요.
I found solace in the fact that I wasn't alone.
위안을 얻다 = to find solace
반려동물이 곁에 있는 것만으로도 위안이 돼요.
Just having my pet by my side is a comfort.
것만으로도 = just by ~ alone
nuance: 위안 is comfort or consolation, the gentle easing of a sad or anxious heart, often from words, presence, or small everyday things. The go-to phrase is 위안이 되다 ('to be a comfort'). It overlaps with 위로, but 위로 emphasizes the act of consoling someone, while 위안 is the inner solace one receives or finds.
mistakes: Mixing it with 위로; 위로 is the act of consoling, 위안 is the comfort felt
Saying 위안하다 for 'to comfort someone'; that role belongs to 위로하다

usage: the easing of tension after worry passes
안도의 한숨을 쉬다 = to sigh in relief
examples: 검사 결과가 정상이라는 말에 안도의 한숨을 쉬었어요.
At the word that the test results were normal, I let out a sigh of relief.
안도의 한숨을 쉬다 = to sigh in relief
아이가 무사히 집에 도착해서 그제야 안도했어요.
My child got home safely, and only then did I feel relieved.
그제야 = only then
일이 잘 끝났다는 소식에 큰 안도감을 느꼈어요.
I felt great relief at the news that everything went well.
안도감을 느끼다 = to feel relief
nuance: 안도 is relief, the loosening of tension once a worry or danger has passed. The signature phrase is 안도의 한숨을 쉬다 ('to breathe a sigh of relief'), and 안도감 names the felt emotion. It is a bit more written and composed than the casual 다행이다 ('what a relief'), which is what you'd blurt out in conversation.
mistakes: Using 안도 in casual speech where 다행이다 is more natural
Confusing 안도 (relief after worry) with 안심 (feeling secure/at ease going forward)

usage: the clinical illness, not just a mood
examples: 비가 며칠째 와서 그런지 기분이 좀 우울해요.
Maybe because it's rained for days, I feel a bit down.
우울하다 = to feel down
요즘 별일 없는데도 우울감이 자주 들어요.
Lately I often feel low even though nothing's wrong.
우울감이 들다 = to feel down
우울할 땐 햇빛을 좀 쐬는 게 도움이 돼요.
When I feel down, getting some sunlight helps.
우울할 때 = when feeling down
nuance: 우울 most often appears as the adjective 우울하다 ('to feel down, gloomy'), the everyday word for a low mood. Be careful to separate the passing feeling 우울하다/우울감 from 우울증, which is clinical depression as a diagnosed condition. Korean 20-30s use 우울하다 freely for ordinary blue days, much like English 'I feel down.'
mistakes: Calling a passing low mood 우울증; that word means clinical depression as an illness
Saying 우울다; the adjective is 우울하다, and the casual form is 우울해요

usage: to feel a sense of injustice
formal; to appeal that one was wronged
examples: 하지도 않은 일로 혼나서 너무 억울했어요.
I got scolded for something I didn't even do, so it felt so unfair.
억울하다 = to feel wronged
제 잘못이 아닌데 오해를 받아서 억울함이 컸어요.
It wasn't my fault but I was misunderstood, so the sense of injustice was great.
오해를 받다 = to be misunderstood
억울하면 참지 말고 차분히 설명하는 게 좋아요.
If you feel wronged, it's better to explain calmly than to bottle it up.
억울하면 = if you feel wronged
nuance: 억울함 is the very Korean feeling of being unfairly blamed or wronged, the frustration of being misjudged when you did nothing wrong. The adjective 억울하다 is extremely common in daily speech (억울해요!). There is no tidy English equivalent, which makes it a valuable word; it centers on injustice done to you, unlike plain 화 (anger).
mistakes: Equating it with simple anger; 억울함 specifically means feeling unjustly wronged
Using 억울함 for general unfairness in the world; it's about a wrong done to you personally, while 불공평 is broad unfairness

usage: deep shame over loss of dignity
examples: 많은 사람들 앞에서 실수해서 수치심을 느꼈어요.
I made a mistake in front of many people, so I felt ashamed.
수치심을 느끼다 = to feel shame
거짓말이 들통나자 큰 수치심이 들었어요.
When the lie was exposed, I was overcome with shame.
수치심이 들다 = shame arises
남을 함부로 대하는 건 정말 수치스러운 일이에요.
Treating others carelessly is a truly shameful thing.
수치스럽다 = to be shameful
nuance: 수치심 is heavy, dignity-wounding shame, far stronger than the everyday 부끄러움 (mild embarrassment). It is the deep disgrace of having one's pride or honor damaged, and shows up in serious contexts. For blushing over a small social slip, use 부끄럽다 or 창피하다; reserve 수치심 for genuine, weighty shame.
mistakes: Using 수치심 for mild embarrassment; that's 부끄러움 or 창피함, while 수치심 is grave shame
Saying 수치심하다; pair the noun with 느끼다/들다, and use 수치스럽다 for the adjective
